newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen easily meeting 1997 borrowing needs.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen easily meeting 1997 borrowing needs.

text.p: Mexico will easily meet its debt needs for 1997, and will likely borrow more than it needs for 1997 to help with a heavy repayment schedule in 1998 and 1999, economists said.

The federal Mexican government and some state agencies will have about $9.0 billion of debt coming due next year, but close to $5.0 billion of that is owed under multilateral or bilateral arrangements that could be renegotiated.
They will have to go to capital markets for the rest.
"The amounts coming due next year are not a problem. It is not a huge amount in the larger context. Mexico could easily find twice that amount," said Bear Stearns fixed-income economist Tulio Vera.
Next year, the Mexican government must go to the markets for about $1.4 billion, while export development bank Bancomext will need about $900 million and development bank Nafin about $800 million.
State-oil company Pemex needs about $830 million, and the Federal Electricity Commission needs $100 million, the Finance Ministry said recently.

But with Banco de Mexico facing payments of $3.3 billion in 1998 and $6.0 billion in 1999 to the International Monetary Fund, Mexico may take advantage of good market conditions to place more paper early to meet those payments.
"They will likely try to profit from the good conditions (next year) to place more issues for the high amortizations with the IMF that they face," said Santander Investment economist Enrique Ramirez.
For the rest of this year, Mexico's sovereign borrowing schedule is almost completed.

A $1.5 billion dual Cetes/Libor note is coming due in November, and but Mexico has already placed a German mark eight-year bond worth about $675 million, then followed it last week with a six-year yen issue worth about $640 million.
"It is not strictly necessary that they will place another issue this year, but they could if conditions are favorable," Ramirez said.
Analysts say that would pose little problem, given the huge success Mexico has had since returning to capital markets after the crushing devaluation of the peso in December 1994.
Mexico placed several smaller issues this year but also a couple of large ones that surprised many observers with their imaginative approach.
In May, it made a blockbuster swap of Brady par and discount bonds for $1.75 billion in uncollateralized 30-year bonds.
In July, Mexico issued $6.0 billion in floating-rate notes, which garnered an investment grade rating on the strength of oil revenues.
That allowed Mexico to speed up its repayments of emergency funds that it received from the United States and to pay off $1.0 billion to the International Monetary Fund.
The recent restructuring of debt has also helped lengthen maturities and cut interest costs.
